# LiveSafe ML pipeline (real NCRB data)

This replaces the previous hand-authored demo dataset (`hotspots_v5.ts`'s old
"AUTO-GENERATED by LiveSafe ML Pipeline v5.0 ... CV Accuracy 0.9566" header,
and the backend's hardcoded `/ml/metrics` numbers) with a real, reproducible
pipeline built from two uploaded NCRB CSVs. Nothing here was fabricated;
every number is either copied straight from the source data or computed by
the scripts in this folder — re-run them and you'll get the same numbers.

## What was fake, and what's real now

| | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Hotspot map | 116 hand-typed cities, `unemployment`/`poverty_mpce`/`chargesheet_rate` fields with no source | 445 real districts, geocoded against an open dataset, real Census population, real NCRB severity |
| "ML model" | Claimed XGBoost+LightGBM+RandomForest ensemble, 96.5% CV accuracy — no such code existed anywhere in the repo | A real GradientBoostingRegressor (`02_train_model.py`), evaluated on a true temporal holdout, metrics reported honestly including where it *doesn't* beat a naive baseline |
| `/ml/metrics` endpoint | Hardcoded literals, never computed from anything | Real metrics from `model_metrics.json` |
| `hotspots` DB table | Did not exist — every Supabase fetch silently failed and fell back to the fake data | Added (`lib/db/src/schema/hotspots.ts`) with a seed script |

## Pipeline

Run in order (each writes files this directory, consumed by the next step):

```bash
cd ml-pipeline
pip install pandas numpy scikit-learn
python3 01_build_master.py     # normalize + geocode + merge population
python3 02_train_model.py      # train + evaluate the real model
python3 03_export_hotspots.py  # export hotspots_real.json + state_summary_real.json
```

Source data (bundled in this folder so the pipeline is reproducible without
external downloads):
- `ncrb_district_year_features.csv` / `ncrb_canonical_long.csv` — the NCRB
  district-year data you provided (1,326 districts × years 2010–2024;
  gaps in 2015–2019 and 2021 reflect actual NCRB publication gaps, not a
  processing error).
- `cities_geo.csv` — [Vynex/indian-cities-geodata](https://github.com/Vynex/indian-cities-geodata)
  (public, itself sourced from Census + Google Maps), used only to attach
  real lat/lon to districts by matching district names to their largest
  city (population > 100k).
- `census2011.csv` — [Census 2011 district data](https://github.com/nishusharma1608/India-Census-2011-Analysis),
  used only for real district population (needed for `crime_rate_per_lakh`).

### 01_build_master.py — normalization & geocoding

- Normalizes district/state names (lowercase, strips "district"/"rural"/
  "commissionerate" suffixes, handles known renames like Trivandrum→
  Thiruvananthapuram via an explicit alias table — see `lib_geo.py`).
- Flags rows that are NCRB reporting units, not real places (Railways, GRP,
  CID, "Total" rows, etc. — 169 of 1,326) and excludes them from the map.
- Matches remaining districts against the geodata source: **445 of 1,326
  (34%) got a real, verified lat/lon.** The rest are genuinely rural
  districts with no city above the 100k-population threshold in the source
  dataset — they are **omitted from the map, not given an invented
  coordinate.** They're still included in `state_summary_real.json`, which
  rolls up all 1,326 districts by state and needs no geocoding.
- Fuzzy matching uses a difflib similarity cutoff of 0.87 after an earlier,
  looser pass produced two false positives caught by manual review (South
  24 Parganas ≠ North 24 Parganas; Agar ≠ Sagar) — both are now explicitly
  blocklisted in `lib_geo.py` rather than risk showing one district's real
  crime data at a different district's coordinates.

### 02_train_model.py — the actual model

- Target: `target_severity` (the source data's own next-year composite
  severity score, 0–1).
- Features: 65 (the engineered NCRB columns — crime counts, state-percentile
  ranks, YoY growth/prev-year values/reporting gaps — plus one-hot state).
- **True temporal holdout**: train on rows where `target_year<=2022`
  (4,888 rows), test on `target_year` in {2023, 2024} (1,895 rows) — the
  model never sees 2023/2024 data during training.
- Model: `GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=3,
  learning_rate=0.05, subsample=0.8)`.

**Honest results:**

| Metric | Model | Naive "next year = this year" baseline |
|---|---|---|
| R² (holdout) | 0.886 | **0.929** |
| MAE (holdout) | 0.061 | **0.048** |
| Risk-class accuracy | 0.777 | **0.825** |
| Risk-class weighted F1 | 0.772 | **0.825** |

**The model does not decisively beat the naive baseline.** This is a real
finding, not a shortcoming to hide: district-level crime severity is highly
persistent year-over-year (helped by `severity` itself being 84% of the
model's feature importance), so a trained model adds limited lift over
simple persistence in this holdout window — plausibly because 2023/2024
directly follow real gaps in NCRB publication (no 2021 data), which widens
the effective forecast horizon for many districts. Where the model *does*
add value: it captures some of the ~18-23% of districts whose risk class
changed year-over-year, which pure persistence by definition cannot.
5-fold CV on the training period alone gives R²=0.876 ± 0.005, consistent
with the holdout number (i.e. no dramatic overfitting).

Full metrics, including precision/recall and top feature importances:
`model_metrics.json`.

### 03_export_hotspots.py — output

- `hotspots_real.json` — 445 real, geocoded districts in the shape the
  frontend expects (see `artifacts/livesafe/src/app/services/hotspots_v5.ts`).
  `risk_score` is the real observed NCRB severity (not a model output).
  `predicted_next_year_severity` / `predicted_next_year_risk_level` are the
  trained model's forecast, given the honesty caveat above.
- `state_summary_real.json` — all 39 states/UTs, no geocoding required,
  for a choropleth or ranking view that doesn't depend on the 34% match
  rate above.

## Limitations (stated plainly)

- **34% district geocoding coverage.** Rural districts without a city over
  100k population aren't on the map. This is a real constraint of the free
  geodata source, not a bug — it was chosen over inventing coordinates.
- **`crime_rate_per_lakh` is null for districts without a Census 2011
  match** (about the same set as ungeocoded ones) — again, left null
  rather than guessed.
- **NCRB reports 5 broad crime heads** (IPC, SLL, crimes against women,
  crimes against children, cyber), not granular offence types like
  "assault" or "murder". The old demo data invented specific offence types
  the source data doesn't support; `predicted_crimes` now uses the real
  NCRB categories (`ipc_crime`, `sll_crime`, `crime_against_women`,
  `crime_against_children`, `cybercrime`) — see the `CrimeType` extension
  in `artifacts/livesafe/src/types/index.ts`.
- **The forecasting model doesn't beat a naive baseline** (see above) —
  reported honestly rather than cherry-picked.
- Delhi is reported by NCRB as police zones (East/West/Central/etc.), not
  one "Delhi" district, so it doesn't appear as a single geocoded point;
  the `/ml/predict` heuristic's "Delhi NCR" base risk uses the mean
  severity across its real zones instead.

## Regenerating after new NCRB data

Replace `ncrb_district_year_features.csv` in this folder and re-run all
three scripts. To push the refreshed data live:
- Frontend (works with no backend): copy the regenerated
  `hotspots_v5_generated.ts`-style output into
  `artifacts/livesafe/src/app/services/hotspots_v5.ts` (see the header
  comment in that file for the exact regeneration command).
- Backend (once a Postgres DB is provisioned): `pnpm --filter
  @workspace/scripts seed-hotspots` loads `hotspots_real.json` into the
  new `hotspots` table (`lib/db/src/schema/hotspots.ts`), which the
  frontend's `supabase.from('hotspots').select('*')` call will pick up
  automatically once it exists (previously it always failed since the
  table didn't exist).
